courses.title: English Language Arts 7
courses.description: A literature-rich seventh-grade course built around short stories, a classic novel, poetry, Shakespearean drama, historical fiction and high-interest nonfiction. Students write narratives, literary analyses, argumentative essays and a research paper, while weekly grammar (phrases, clauses, sentence variety, modifiers) and Greek/Latin word study are woven into the reading. Speaking and listening grow through discussions, a dramatic reading, a debate and a multimedia presentation.
courses.framework: California Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts & Literacy; 2014 CA ELA/ELD Framework

standards.RL.7.1: Cite several pieces of textual evidence to support analysis of what a literary text says explicitly and by inference.
standards.RL.7.2: Determine a theme or central idea of a text and analyze its development; provide an objective summary.
standards.RL.7.3: Analyze how particular elements of a story or drama interact (e.g., how setting shapes characters or plot).
standards.RL.7.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases, including figurative and connotative meanings; analyze the impact of rhymes and repetitions of sounds.
standards.RL.7.5: Analyze how a drama's or poem's form or structure (e.g., soliloquy, sonnet) contributes to its meaning.
standards.RL.7.6: Analyze how an author develops and contrasts the points of view of different characters or narrators.
standards.RL.7.7: Compare and contrast a written story, drama or poem to its audio, filmed, staged or multimedia version.
standards.RL.7.9: Compare and contrast a fictional portrayal of a time, place or character and a historical account of the same period.
standards.RL.7.10: Read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas and poems, in the grades 6–8 complexity band proficiently.
standards.RI.7.1: Cite several pieces of textual evidence to support analysis of what an informational text says explicitly and by inference.
standards.RI.7.2: Determine two or more central ideas in a text and analyze their development; provide an objective summary.
standards.RI.7.3: Analyze the interactions between individuals, events and ideas in a text.
standards.RI.7.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases in informational text, including figurative, connotative and technical meanings.
standards.RI.7.5: Analyze the structure an author uses to organize a text and how major sections contribute to the whole.
standards.RI.7.6: Determine an author's point of view or purpose and analyze how the author distinguishes his or her position from others'.
standards.RI.7.7: Compare and contrast a text to an audio, video or multimedia version, analyzing each medium's portrayal of the subject.
standards.RI.7.8: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing whether reasoning is sound and evidence relevant and sufficient.
standards.RI.7.9: Analyze how two or more authors writing about the same topic shape their presentations by emphasizing different evidence or interpretations.
standards.RI.7.10: Read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 6–8 complexity band proficiently.
standards.W.7.1: Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence, acknowledging alternate or opposing claims.
standards.W.7.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine a topic and convey ideas through selection, organization and analysis of relevant content.
standards.W.7.3: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences using effective technique, relevant details and well-structured event sequences.
standards.W.7.4: Produce clear and coherent writing appropriate to task, purpose and audience.
standards.W.7.5: Develop and strengthen writing by planning, revising, editing, rewriting or trying a new approach.
standards.W.7.6: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce and publish writing and link to and cite sources.
standards.W.7.7: Conduct short research projects to answer a question, drawing on several sources and generating additional focused questions.
standards.W.7.8: Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources; assess credibility; quote or paraphrase while avoiding plagiarism; follow a standard citation format.
standards.W.7.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection and research.
standards.W.7.10: Write routinely over extended and shorter time frames for a range of tasks and purposes.
standards.SL.7.1: Engage effectively in a range of collaborative discussions, building on others' ideas and expressing one's own clearly.
standards.SL.7.2: Analyze the main ideas and supporting details presented in diverse media and formats and explain how they clarify a topic.
standards.SL.7.3: Delineate a speaker's argument and specific claims, evaluating the soundness of reasoning and relevance of evidence.
standards.SL.7.4: Present claims and findings, emphasizing salient points in a focused, coherent manner with pertinent evidence, eye contact, adequate volume and clear pronunciation.
standards.SL.7.5: Include multimedia components and visual displays in presentations to clarify claims and findings.
standards.SL.7.6: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when appropriate.
standards.L.7.1a: Explain the function of phrases and clauses in general and their function in specific sentences.
standards.L.7.1b: Choose among simple, compound, complex and compound-complex sentences to signal differing relationships among ideas.
standards.L.7.1c: Place phrases and clauses within a sentence, recognizing and correcting misplaced and dangling modifiers.
standards.L.7.2a: Use a comma to separate coordinate adjectives.
standards.L.7.3a: Choose language that expresses ideas precisely and concisely, eliminating wordiness and redundancy.
standards.L.7.4a: Use context as a clue to the meaning of a word or phrase.
standards.L.7.4b: Use common, grade-appropriate Greek or Latin affixes and roots as clues to the meaning of a word.
standards.L.7.4c: Consult reference materials to find pronunciation and clarify precise meaning or part of speech.
standards.L.7.5a: Interpret figures of speech (e.g., literary, biblical and mythological allusions) in context.
standards.L.7.5b: Use the relationship between particular words (synonym/antonym, analogy) to better understand each.
standards.L.7.5c: Distinguish among the connotations of words with similar denotations.
standards.L.7.6: Acquire and use accurately grade-appropriate general academic and domain-specific words and phrases.

weeks.topic: Launching the year; 'Thank You, Ma'am' by Langston Hughes
objectives: Analyze how characters' actions reveal traits

days.title: Reader inventory
days.work: Complete a reading interest survey, set a goal of 25 independent books for the year, and write a journal entry about a memorable story.

days.title: Read 'Thank You, Ma'am'
days.work: Read Hughes' 'Thank You, Ma'am' aloud and annotate Mrs. Jones's actions and words with sticky notes labeled 'trait' and 'evidence'.

days.title: Direct vs. indirect characterization
days.work: Build a two-column chart of direct and indirect characterization for Roger and Mrs. Jones and write a paragraph on how she changes him, citing two quotes.

days.title: Grammar: phrases vs. clauses
days.work: Learn phrases (prepositional, participial) versus independent and dependent clauses and label 15 sentences from the story.

days.title: Discussion & check
days.work: Discuss with a parent whether Mrs. Jones's choice was wise, building on each other's points, then take a short quiz on characterization and clauses.

weeks.assessment: Evidence paragraph, grammar labeling and discussion checklist.

weeks.topic: Suspense: 'The Most Dangerous Game' by Richard Connell
objectives: Analyze how setting shapes conflict and plot
Use Greek/Latin roots to define words

days.title: Ship-Trap Island
days.work: Read the first third of 'The Most Dangerous Game' and list details of setting that create a sense of danger.

days.title: Rising action
days.work: Read the middle section and chart Rainsford's three tricks on a plot diagram, noting foreshadowing clues.

days.title: Climax and ending
days.work: Finish the story and write a paragraph explaining how the jungle setting drives the conflict, with three cited details.

days.title: Word study: roots
days.work: Study roots 'mal', 'bene', 'vis/vid', 'dict' and 'port'; find story words and build a 15-word root web.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a reading quiz with two constructed responses and a 10-item root quiz.

weeks.assessment: Plot diagram, setting paragraph, reading and root quizzes.

weeks.topic: Point of view: 'The Tell-Tale Heart' by Edgar Allan Poe

days.title: Listen and read

days.title: Unreliable narrator
days.work: Make a T-chart of what the narrator claims versus what his actions show and explain why he is unreliable.

days.title: Mood and word choice
days.work: Identify repetition, dashes and sound words that build tension and explain their effect on mood in a paragraph.

days.title: Grammar: coordinate adjectives
days.work: Learn the comma rule for coordinate adjectives (the 'and' test) and edit 12 sentences describing the old man's room.

days.title: Rewrite & check

objectives: Plan and draft a personal narrative with conflict
Use dialogue, pacing and sensory detail

days.title: Planning

days.title: Drafting the opening

days.title: Drafting the body

days.title: Peer conference
days.work: Read the draft aloud to a parent who gives two 'glows' and one 'grow'; record revision goals.

weeks.assessment: Complete narrative draft and revision goals.

objectives: Revise for pacing and word choice
Analyze theme in a short story

days.title: Revision: pacing
days.work: Revise the narrative using a checklist: add transitions, cut one slow section, expand the climax.

days.title: Editing & publishing
days.work: Edit for clauses, commas and spelling, then type and publish the final narrative.

days.title: Read 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi'
days.work: Read Kipling's 'Rikki-Tikki-Tavi' and track how Rikki's courage develops through each conflict.

days.title: Theme statement
days.work: Write an objective summary of the story and a theme statement supported by three pieces of evidence.

days.title: Unit 1 assessment
days.work: Take a unit test on an unseen short story (CommonLit) with questions on plot, character, point of view and theme.

weeks.assessment: Published personal narrative (rubric) and unit 1 test.

days.title: Objective summary

objectives: Write a literary analysis with embedded quotations

days.title: Conclusion & revision
days.work: Draft a conclusion and revise transitions between paragraphs for cohesion.

days.title: Editing
days.work: Edit for sentence variety, quotation punctuation and spelling, then publish the essay.

days.title: Unit 2 assessment

days.title: Objective summary

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on an unseen article identifying structure and central ideas.

objectives: Evaluate evidence for relevance and sufficiency

days.title: Anatomy of an argument

days.title: Sound reasoning?

days.work: Analyze how the author distinguishes her view from opponents' using specific phrases.

days.title: Listening to arguments

days.title: Review & check

weeks.topic: Paired texts: same topic, different authors
objectives: Compare how two authors present the same topic
materials: two articles on zoos (pro and con)

days.title: Text A
days.work: Read an article arguing zoos protect endangered species and highlight evidence types (statistics, expert, anecdote).

days.title: Text B
days.work: Read an article arguing zoos harm animals and highlight its evidence the same way.

days.title: Compare authors
days.work: Write a comparison paragraph on how each author emphasizes different evidence and facts.

days.title: Taking a position
days.work: Choose a position on 'Should zoos exist?' and fill an evidence organizer with at least 5 pieces of evidence.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Draft a claim and counterclaim statement and get feedback.

objectives: Write a claim-based essay with counterclaim and rebuttal

days.title: Introduction
days.work: Draft an introduction with background and a clear claim.

days.title: Reasons and evidence
days.work: Draft two body paragraphs, each with a reason, two pieces of cited evidence and explanation.

days.title: Counterclaim
days.work: Draft a counterclaim and rebuttal paragraph using phrases like 'Some argue… however…'.

days.work: Cut wordiness and redundancy from 12 practice sentences, then from your own draft.

days.title: Conclusion
days.work: Draft a conclusion that restates the claim and leaves a call to action.

days.title: Revision
days.work: Revise for logical order and transitions using a color-coding check (claim, evidence, reasoning).

days.title: Editing & citations
days.work: Edit grammar and add in-text citations, then publish the final essay.

days.title: Oral argument

days.title: Reflection

days.title: Unit 3 assessment

days.title: Sound devices

days.title: Review & check

materials: Frost: 'The Road Not Taken', 'Nothing Gold Can Stay'

days.title: The sonnet
days.work: Read Sonnet 18, map its three quatrains and couplet, and explain how the couplet turns the argument.

days.title: Frost
days.work: Read 'The Road Not Taken' and 'Nothing Gold Can Stay' and write a theme statement for each.

days.title: Free verse vs. rhyme

days.title: Poem vs. performance
days.work: Listen to a recorded reading of a poem and compare how the reader's voice changes its meaning (RL.7.7).

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a 1-page analysis of how form shapes meaning in one poem from the week.

objectives: Write original poems using devices and forms

days.title: Imagery poem

days.title: Form poem

days.title: Figurative poem

days.title: Recitation practice

courses.title: Mathematics 7
courses.description: Grade 7 mathematics centered on proportional reasoning, operations with rational numbers, expressions and equations, geometry of scale, circles, angles, area, surface area and volume, and probability and sampling. The sequence mirrors the Illustrative Mathematics Grade 7 scope used by many California districts, with rich tasks, number talks, and real-world modeling aligned to the 2023 CA Mathematics Framework's big ideas.
courses.framework: California Common Core State Standards for Mathematics; 2023 CA Mathematics Framework

standards.7.RP.A.1: Compute unit rates associated with ratios of fractions, including ratios of lengths, areas and other quantities.
standards.7.RP.A.2: Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities.
standards.7.RP.A.2a: Decide whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship using tables or graphs through the origin.
standards.7.RP.A.2b: Identify the constant of proportionality (unit rate) in tables, graphs, equations, diagrams and verbal descriptions.
standards.7.RP.A.2c: Represent proportional relationships by equations such as y = kx.
standards.7.RP.A.2d: Explain what a point (x, y) on the graph of a proportional relationship means, including (0,0) and (1, r).
standards.7.RP.A.3: Use proportional relationships to solve multistep ratio and percent problems (tax, tips, markups, discounts, interest, percent error).
standards.7.NS.A.1: Apply and extend understandings of addition and subtraction to add and subtract rational numbers; represent on a number line.
standards.7.NS.A.2: Apply and extend understandings of multiplication and division to multiply and divide rational numbers.
standards.7.NS.A.2d: Convert a rational number to a decimal using long division; know it terminates or repeats.
standards.7.NS.A.3: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the four operations with rational numbers.
standards.7.EE.A.1: Apply properties of operations to add, subtract, factor and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients.
standards.7.EE.A.2: Understand that rewriting an expression in different forms can shed light on how quantities are related.
standards.7.EE.B.3: Solve multistep real-life problems with positive and negative rational numbers in any form; assess reasonableness with estimation.
standards.7.EE.B.4: Use variables to represent quantities and construct simple equations and inequalities to solve problems.
standards.7.EE.B.4a: Solve word problems leading to equations px + q = r and p(x + q) = r fluently; compare algebraic and arithmetic solutions.
standards.7.EE.B.4b: Solve word problems leading to inequalities px + q > r or px + q < r; graph and interpret the solution set.
standards.7.G.A.1: Solve problems involving scale drawings of geometric figures, including computing actual lengths and areas and reproducing a drawing at a different scale.
standards.7.G.A.2: Draw geometric shapes with given conditions; construct triangles from three measures of angles or sides and note when a unique triangle results.
standards.7.G.A.3: Describe the two-dimensional figures that result from slicing three-dimensional figures.
standards.7.G.B.4: Know and use the formulas for the area and circumference of a circle; give an informal derivation of the relationship.
standards.7.G.B.5: Use facts about supplementary, complementary, vertical and adjacent angles to write and solve equations for an unknown angle.
standards.7.G.B.6: Solve real-world problems involving area, volume and surface area of 2-D and 3-D objects composed of triangles, quadrilaterals, polygons, cubes and right prisms.
standards.7.SP.A.1: Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a representative sample; random sampling.
standards.7.SP.A.2: Use data from a random sample to draw inferences about a population; gauge variation in estimates from multiple samples.
standards.7.SP.B.3: Informally assess the degree of visual overlap of two numerical data distributions with similar variabilities.
standards.7.SP.B.4: Use measures of center and variability from random samples to draw informal comparative inferences about two populations.
standards.7.SP.C.5: Understand that the probability of a chance event is a number between 0 and 1 expressing likelihood.
standards.7.SP.C.6: Approximate the probability of a chance event by collecting data and observing long-run relative frequency.
standards.7.SP.C.7: Develop a probability model and use it to find probabilities of events; compare to observed frequencies.
standards.7.SP.C.8: Find probabilities of compound events using organized lists, tables, tree diagrams and simulation.

units.title: Scale Drawings
units.big_idea: Scaled copies keep angles and multiply every length by the same scale factor; areas scale by the square of the factor.

units.title: Introducing Proportional Relationships
units.big_idea: A proportional relationship has a constant of proportionality that appears in tables, equations y = kx and graphs through the origin.

units.title: Measuring Circles
units.big_idea: Circumference is proportional to diameter with constant pi; area of a circle is pi r squared.

units.title: Proportional Relationships and Percentages
units.big_idea: Percent change, tax, tips, discounts, interest and error are all proportional reasoning.

units.title: Rational Number Arithmetic
units.big_idea: Positive and negative numbers obey consistent rules for all four operations, modeled with number lines and real contexts.

units.title: Expressions, Equations, and Inequalities
units.big_idea: Equivalent expressions and balanced equations let us solve for unknowns; inequalities describe ranges of solutions.

units.title: Angles, Triangles, and Prisms
units.big_idea: Angle relationships produce equations; triangles are determined by certain measures; prisms have measurable surface area and volume.

units.title: Probability and Sampling
units.big_idea: Probability measures likelihood; random samples let us make inferences and compare populations.

days.work: Build intersecting lines with paper strips and a brad to show vertical angles stay equal as you rotate.

days.title: Angle equations
days.work: Solve 10 problems like (2x + 10) + 3x = 180 from diagrams.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on angle relationships and equations.

objectives: Determine when conditions give a unique triangle

days.title: Building with straws
days.work: Cut straws to given lengths and test which sets of three form a triangle; state the triangle inequality.

days.title: Angle conditions
days.work: Try to draw triangles with angles 50, 60, 70 and note that many sizes exist (not unique).

days.title: Side-angle-side
days.work: Construct triangles from two sides and the included angle using ruler and protractor and compare with a sibling's copy.

days.title: Unique or not?
days.work: Classify 8 sets of conditions as giving no triangle, one unique triangle, or many triangles.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on triangle constructions.

weeks.topic: Cross sections and volume of prisms

days.title: Slicing solids
days.work: Shape clay into a cube, cylinder and pyramid and slice with floss parallel and perpendicular to the base; sketch each cross section.

days.title: Volume of prisms
days.work: Find volume as area of base times height for rectangular and triangular prisms.

days.title: Composite prisms
days.work: Find the volume of a step-shaped and L-shaped prism by decomposing.

days.title: Measuring real prisms
days.work: Measure a cereal box and a triangular Toblerone-style box and compute their volumes.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on cross sections and prism volume.

objectives: Find surface area of prisms using nets
Distinguish surface area from volume problems

days.title: Nets
days.work: Draw and cut out nets of a triangular and a rectangular prism and fold them to check.

days.title: Surface area
days.work: Find surface area of prisms from nets and from dimensions, including a prism with a hole.

days.title: Which measure?
days.work: Decide whether 8 situations (wrapping a gift, filling a pool) need surface area or volume, then solve them.

days.title: Unit review
days.work: Mixed review of angles, triangles, cross sections, surface area and volume.

days.title: Unit 7 test
days.work: Take the unit 7 test.

objectives: Describe probability as a number from 0 to 1

days.title: Likelihood
days.work: Place 10 events on a 0-to-1 likelihood line from impossible to certain and justify placement.

days.title: Sample spaces
days.work: List sample spaces for rolling a die, flipping two coins and spinning a 4-color spinner.

days.title: Experimental probability
days.work: Draw from a bag of colored tiles 50 times with replacement and compute relative frequencies.

days.title: Theory vs experiment
days.work: Compare results to theoretical probability and explain how more trials bring them closer.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on probability language and models.

days.title: Tree diagrams
days.work: Draw tree diagrams for outfit choices and coin-die combinations and count outcomes.

days.title: Tables of outcomes
days.work: Make a 6x6 table of sums of two dice and find P(sum = 7) and P(doubles).

days.title: Designing a simulation
days.work: Design a coin-flip simulation for 'a family with 3 children has at least 2 girls' and run 30 trials.

days.title: Simulating with technology
days.work: Use a random number generator to simulate a 30% free-throw shooter taking 5 shots and estimate P(at least 2 makes).

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on compound events and simulation design.

weeks.assessment: Compound probability quiz and simulation write-up.

objectives: Compare two populations with measures of center and variability

days.title: Populations and samples
days.work: Identify populations and samples in 8 survey scenarios and judge which are biased.

days.title: Random sampling
days.work: Use random page numbers to sample word lengths in a novel and estimate the mean word length.

days.title: Variation in samples
days.work: Take 5 random samples of 10 words, compare sample means and describe the variability.

days.title: Comparing groups
days.work: Compare two dot plots (e.g., heights of two plant groups) using means and MAD and decide if the difference is meaningful.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on sampling and comparing populations.

weeks.assessment: Sampling quiz and word-length sampling report.

days.title: Plan an investigation
days.work: Write a statistical question comparing two groups (e.g., reaction times of kids vs adults) and plan a random sample.

days.title: Collect and display
days.work: Collect data from at least 10 people per group with a ruler-drop test and create dot plots or box plots.

days.title: Analyze and report
days.work: Compute means and MADs, write conclusions, and present findings to the family.

days.work: Complete a cumulative review covering all 8 units.

courses.subject: SCI
courses.title: Science 7 (Integrated)
courses.description: Grade 7 integrated science following the California preferred integrated model: matter is made of atoms that rearrange in chemical reactions, matter cycles and energy flows through organisms and ecosystems, Earth's materials cycle and its surface records a long history, and humans must sustain biodiversity and resources. Every week includes a hands-on investigation with household materials, science notebooks with claim-evidence-reasoning writing, and engineering design challenges.
courses.framework: California Next Generation Science Standards (CA NGSS); 2016 CA Science Framework, Grade 7 Preferred Integrated Model

standards.MS-PS1-1: Develop models to describe the atomic composition of simple molecules and extended structures.
standards.MS-PS1-2: Analyze and interpret data on the properties of substances before and after interaction to determine if a chemical reaction occurred.
standards.MS-PS1-3: Gather and make sense of information to describe that synthetic materials come from natural resources and impact society.
standards.MS-PS1-5: Develop and use a model to describe how the total number of atoms does not change in a chemical reaction and thus mass is conserved.
standards.MS-PS1-6: Undertake a design project to construct, test and modify a device that either releases or absorbs thermal energy by chemical processes.
standards.MS-LS1-6: Construct a scientific explanation based on evidence for the role of photosynthesis in the cycling of matter and flow of energy into and out of organisms.
standards.MS-LS1-7: Develop a model to describe how food is rearranged through chemical reactions forming new molecules that support growth and/or release energy.
standards.MS-LS2-1: Analyze and interpret data to provide evidence for the effects of resource availability on organisms and populations in an ecosystem.
standards.MS-LS2-2: Construct an explanation that predicts patterns of interactions among organisms across multiple ecosystems.
standards.MS-LS2-3: Develop a model to describe the cycling of matter and flow of energy among living and nonliving parts of an ecosystem.
standards.MS-LS2-4: Construct an argument supported by empirical evidence that changes to physical or biological components of an ecosystem affect populations.
standards.MS-LS2-5: Evaluate competing design solutions for maintaining biodiversity and ecosystem services.
standards.MS-LS4-1: Analyze and interpret data for patterns in the fossil record that document the existence, diversity, extinction and change of life forms.
standards.MS-ESS1-4: Construct a scientific explanation based on evidence from rock strata for how the geologic time scale is used to organize Earth's 4.6-billion-year history.
standards.MS-ESS2-1: Develop a model to describe the cycling of Earth's materials and the flow of energy that drives this process.
standards.MS-ESS2-2: Construct an explanation based on evidence for how geoscience processes have changed Earth's surface at varying time and spatial scales.
standards.MS-ESS2-3: Analyze and interpret data on the distribution of fossils and rocks, continental shapes and seafloor structures to provide evidence of past plate motions.
standards.MS-ESS3-1: Construct a scientific explanation based on evidence for how the uneven distributions of Earth's mineral, energy and groundwater resources are the result of past and current geoscience processes.
standards.MS-ESS3-3: Apply scientific principles to design a method for monitoring and minimizing a human impact on the environment.
standards.MS-ESS3-4: Construct an argument supported by evidence for how increases in human population and per-capita consumption of natural resources impact Earth's systems.
standards.MS-ETS1-1: Define the criteria and constraints of a design problem with sufficient precision to ensure a successful solution.
standards.MS-ETS1-2: Evaluate competing design solutions using a systematic process to determine how well they meet the criteria and constraints.
standards.MS-ETS1-3: Analyze data from tests to determine similarities and differences among several design solutions to identify the best characteristics of each.
standards.MS-ETS1-4: Develop a model to generate data for iterative testing and modification of a proposed object, tool or process.

units.title: Atoms, Molecules and Materials
units.big_idea: All matter, living and nonliving, is made of atoms that combine into molecules and extended structures; people turn natural resources into synthetic materials.

units.title: Chemical Reactions and Conservation of Matter
units.big_idea: In a chemical reaction atoms rearrange into new substances with new properties, mass is conserved, and energy can be released or absorbed.

units.title: Matter and Energy in Organisms
units.big_idea: Plants capture light energy to build sugar from carbon dioxide and water; organisms rearrange food molecules to grow and release energy.

units.title: Ecosystems: Interactions, Matter and Energy
units.big_idea: Resource availability and interactions shape populations; matter cycles and energy flows through ecosystems.

units.title: Earth's Materials and Resources
units.big_idea: Earth's materials cycle through the rock cycle driven by internal heat and the sun, and geologic processes leave resources unevenly distributed.

units.title: Earth's History and Plate Tectonics
units.big_idea: Rock layers, fossils and plate motions record Earth's 4.6-billion-year history at many time and spatial scales.

units.title: Sustaining Biodiversity and Earth's Systems
units.big_idea: Changes to ecosystems affect populations; human population and consumption impact Earth, and engineers design solutions to monitor and reduce those impacts.

weeks.topic: What is everything made of? Particles and atoms
objectives: Use evidence that matter is made of tiny particles
Set up a science notebook and lab safety habits

days.title: Safety & notebook
days.work: Set up a science notebook with a table of contents and sign a home lab safety contract after reviewing goggles, heat and chemical rules.

days.title: Phenomenon: food coloring
days.work: Drop food coloring into hot and cold water, time how long it takes to spread, and sketch a particle model of what is happening.

days.title: Scent in a balloon
days.work: Put vanilla extract inside a balloon, inflate and tie it, then smell the outside and explain using particles.

days.title: Atoms and elements
days.work: Use the PhET 'Build an Atom' simulation to build hydrogen, carbon and oxygen atoms and record protons, neutrons and electrons.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph answering 'Is matter continuous or made of particles?' and take a vocabulary quiz.

weeks.assessment: CER paragraph and particle model sketches.

days.title: Element hunt
days.work: Find 10 elements in household items (aluminum foil, copper wire, carbon pencil lead) and locate them on a periodic table.

days.title: Reading the table
days.work: Identify atomic number, symbol and mass for 15 elements and color-code metals, nonmetals and metalloids.

days.title: Mixtures lab
days.work: Separate a mixture of salt, sand and paper-clip bits using a magnet, filtering and evaporation.

days.title: Compounds vs. mixtures
days.work: Sort 12 substances (water, air, salt, trail mix, sugar) as element, compound or mixture with justification.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Take a quiz on elements, compounds, mixtures and periodic-table reading.

objectives: Contrast molecules with extended structures like salt and diamond

days.title: Chemical formulas
days.work: Interpret formulas H2O, CO2, O2, CH4 and C6H12O6 by counting atoms of each element.

days.title: Gumdrop molecules
days.work: Build gumdrop-and-toothpick models of water, carbon dioxide, methane and ammonia using a color key.

days.title: PhET Build a Molecule
days.work: Use PhET 'Build a Molecule' to assemble 8 molecules and record formulas and names.

days.title: Crystals
days.work: Examine salt and sugar crystals with a magnifier and build a repeating NaCl lattice model to show an extended structure.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Draw labeled models of three molecules and one extended structure and explain the difference.

objectives: Use density, melting point and solubility to identify substances

days.title: Density
days.work: Measure mass and volume of water, oil and corn syrup and calculate density for each.

days.title: Density column
days.work: Build a density column with corn syrup, water and oil and predict where a grape, cork and coin will settle.

days.title: Solubility
days.work: Test how many teaspoons of salt, sugar and baking soda dissolve in 100 mL of water and graph results.

days.title: Mystery powders
days.work: Identify three unlabeled white powders using solubility, texture and reaction with vinegar or iodine.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a lab report on the mystery-powder investigation with a data table and conclusion.

weeks.assessment: Density calculations and mystery-powder lab report.

objectives: Trace synthetic materials back to natural resources
Evaluate societal impact of a synthetic material

days.title: Natural vs. synthetic
days.work: Sort 15 household items as natural or synthetic and trace three synthetics back to their raw resources.

days.title: Milk plastic
days.work: Make casein plastic from warm milk and vinegar, mold it and let it dry.

days.title: Polymer slime
days.work: Make glue-and-borax slime and compare its properties to the starting materials.

days.title: Research a material
days.work: Research nylon, polyester or plastic bags and write how they are made and how they affect society and the environment.

days.title: Unit 1 assessment
days.work: Take the unit 1 test and present a one-page infographic on a synthetic material.

days.title: Phenomenon: rusty nail
days.work: Compare a new and rusted nail and list differences in properties; start a steel-wool rusting jar to observe all week.

days.title: Signs of reactions
days.work: Run four mini-reactions (baking soda + vinegar, milk + lemon juice, Alka-Seltzer + water, steel wool + vinegar) and record evidence.

days.title: Physical vs. chemical
days.work: Test melting ice, dissolving sugar, burning a candle and toasting bread; classify each with evidence.

days.title: Before and after data
days.work: Analyze a data table of properties before and after interactions to decide if new substances formed.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a CER on whether rusting is a chemical reaction using the week's steel-wool observations.

objectives: Model reactions as rearrangements of atoms

days.title: Reading equations
days.work: Identify reactants, products, coefficients and subscripts in five chemical equations.

days.title: Modeling with LEGO
days.work: Use colored LEGO bricks to model methane burning (CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O) and count atoms before and after.

days.title: Balancing simulation
days.work: Complete PhET 'Balancing Chemical Equations' intro and game levels 1–2.

days.title: Baking soda and vinegar equation
days.work: Model the baking soda + vinegar reaction and explain where the gas comes from.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz: count atoms and balance three simple equations with models.

objectives: Collect evidence that mass is conserved

days.title: Open system
days.work: Mass baking soda and vinegar before and after reacting in an open cup and calculate the apparent mass loss.

days.title: Closed system
days.work: Repeat the reaction in a bottle sealed with a balloon and compare before-and-after masses.

days.title: Explaining results
days.work: Draw particle models explaining why mass seemed to change in the open cup but not the sealed bottle.

days.title: Lavoisier
days.work: Read about Antoine Lavoisier's experiments and summarize how he established conservation of mass.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a full lab report with data, graph and conclusion.

weeks.topic: Energy in reactions: hot and cold
objectives: Classify reactions as exothermic or endothermic

days.title: Measuring change
days.work: Measure temperature change for baking soda + vinegar every 30 seconds and graph it.

days.title: Hot reaction
days.work: Measure temperature change for yeast + hydrogen peroxide and for steel wool + vinegar in a jar.

days.title: Comparing reactions
days.work: Compare graphs and classify each reaction as exothermic or endothermic.

days.title: Hand warmers & cold packs
days.work: Read how commercial hand warmers and instant cold packs work and identify their chemicals.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on exothermic and endothermic reactions with graph interpretation.

weeks.topic: Engineering challenge: design a hand warmer or cold pack
objectives: Test, compare and iterate a design

days.title: Define the problem
days.work: Write criteria (e.g., warms 10 °C for 5 minutes) and constraints (safe, cheap, under 50 g) for a chemical warmer or cooler.

days.title: Prototype 1
days.work: Build and test two designs with different amounts of reactants and record temperature over time.

days.title: Analyze and improve
days.work: Compare test data in a decision matrix and redesign to better meet criteria.

days.title: Prototype 2
days.work: Test the improved design three times and calculate the average temperature change.

days.title: Unit 2 assessment
days.work: Present the final design with data and take the unit 2 test.

weeks.topic: Photosynthesis: where does a plant's mass come from?
objectives: Gather evidence about inputs and outputs of photosynthesis

days.title: Phenomenon: a growing tree
days.work: Read about van Helmont's willow tree experiment and predict where the tree's mass came from.

days.title: Floating leaf disks
days.work: Use a syringe to infiltrate spinach leaf disks with baking-soda water and count how many float under a lamp every minute.

days.title: Light variable
days.work: Repeat the leaf-disk test at different lamp distances and graph floating rate versus light.

days.title: Photosynthesis equation
days.work: Build a gumdrop model of 6CO2 + 6H2O → C6H12O6 + 6O2 and explain how atoms are rearranged.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a CER answering 'Where does a plant's mass come from?' using leaf-disk evidence.

objectives: Explain how organisms release energy from food
materials: bromothymol blue or red cabbage indicator

days.title: Yeast balloons
days.work: Feed yeast different amounts of sugar in bottles topped with balloons and measure balloon circumference every 10 minutes.

days.title: Breath test
days.work: Blow through a straw into red-cabbage indicator before and after exercise and compare color changes as evidence of CO2.

days.title: Respiration equation
days.work: Compare photosynthesis and respiration equations and draw a diagram of how they are linked.

days.title: Food to body
days.work: Model how digested food molecules are rearranged to build body tissue or release energy.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on respiration and its relationship to photosynthesis.

objectives: Explain food as fuel and building material

days.title: Nutrient tests
days.work: Test foods for starch with iodine and for fat with brown paper and record results.

days.title: Nutrition labels
days.work: Analyze five nutrition labels to compare calories from carbohydrates, fats and proteins.

days.title: Energy in a peanut (demo)
days.work: With an adult, burn a cheese puff under a can of water and calculate the temperature change as evidence of stored energy.

days.title: Growth and repair
days.work: Read about how proteins are broken into amino acids and rebuilt into body proteins and summarize in a flowchart.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write an explanation of how a sandwich becomes both energy and muscle.

weeks.topic: Matter and energy in organisms: synthesis
objectives: Integrate photosynthesis and respiration in one model
materials: sealed jar with plant and snail (optional)

days.title: Sealed ecosystem
days.work: Analyze data from a sealed jar containing a plant (and optionally a snail) and explain how both survive.

days.title: Carbon atom journey
days.work: Write a story following one carbon atom from the air into a leaf, a rabbit and back into the air.

days.title: Model poster
days.work: Create a poster model linking photosynthesis and respiration with matter and energy arrows.

days.title: Unit review
days.work: Review with flashcards and a practice set on unit 3 concepts.

days.title: Unit 3 assessment
days.work: Take the unit 3 test.

weeks.assessment: Carbon story, model poster and unit 3 test.

objectives: Analyze data on resource availability and population size

days.title: Oh Deer! simulation
days.work: Play a tabletop version of 'Oh Deer!' with beans for food, water and shelter over 15 rounds and graph the deer population.

days.title: Population graphs
days.work: Interpret real data on the lynx-hare population cycle and describe the pattern.

days.title: Crowding experiment
days.work: Plant radish seeds at 3 different densities to investigate competition for resources.

days.title: Carrying capacity
days.work: Analyze a graph of a population reaching carrying capacity and identify limiting factors.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on limiting factors and population graphs.

days.title: Interaction types
days.work: Sort 20 organism-pair cards into predation, competition, mutualism, commensalism and parasitism.

days.title: Backyard survey
days.work: Observe a yard or park for 30 minutes and record organisms and any interactions seen.

days.title: Across ecosystems
days.work: Compare interactions in a kelp forest, desert and tropical rainforest and identify repeating patterns.

days.title: Sea otters
days.work: Read about California sea otters, urchins and kelp and explain the predator-prey pattern.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write an explanation predicting what would happen if a predator were removed from an ecosystem.

objectives: Explain why energy decreases up trophic levels

days.title: Food chains
days.work: Build food chains for a California chaparral ecosystem and label producers, consumers and decomposers.

days.title: Yarn web
days.work: Connect organism cards with yarn into a food web and observe the effect of 'removing' one organism.

days.title: Owl pellet
days.work: Dissect an owl pellet (or virtual pellet) and identify prey bones to build the owl's food web.

days.title: Energy pyramid
days.work: Calculate energy available at each level using the 10% rule and draw an energy pyramid.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on food webs and energy pyramids.

objectives: Model how matter cycles in ecosystems

days.title: Decomposition jars
days.work: Set up decomposition jars with bread, apple and leaves under moist and dry conditions to observe over weeks.

days.title: Mold growth
days.work: Observe moldy bread with a magnifier and draw hyphae and spores.

days.title: Nitrogen and carbon
days.work: Diagram how carbon and nitrogen cycle among plants, animals, decomposers and soil.

days.title: Compost design
days.work: Design a small compost bin and explain how it returns matter to the soil.

days.title: Semester review & check
days.work: Take a cumulative semester 1 checkpoint on units 1–4.

objectives: Build and monitor an ecosystem model

days.title: Build a terrarium
days.work: Build a bottle terrarium with plants, soil, water and small invertebrates and diagram its biotic and abiotic parts.

days.title: Decomposition check
days.work: Record changes in the decomposition jars and explain which conditions sped up decomposition.

days.title: Matter and energy diagram
days.work: Draw arrows showing matter cycling and energy flowing through the terrarium.

days.title: Unit review
days.work: Review unit 4 vocabulary and practice data-analysis questions.

days.title: Unit 4 assessment
days.work: Take the unit 4 test; continue terrarium observation weekly.

days.title: Mineral properties
days.work: Test samples for luster, streak and hardness using a fingernail, penny and nail on the Mohs scale.

days.title: Grow crystals
days.work: Grow salt or sugar crystals from a supersaturated solution and connect to how minerals form.

days.title: Rock types
days.work: Classify yard and store-bought rocks into igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic with an ID key.

days.title: Fizz test
days.work: Test rocks with vinegar to identify limestone/calcite and explain the chemical reaction.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on mineral properties and rock types.

weeks.assessment: Rock and mineral ID chart and quiz.

weeks.topic: The rock cycle and energy that drives it
objectives: Identify the energy sources driving it

days.title: Crayon rock cycle
days.work: Shave crayons into sediment, press into 'sedimentary rock', heat-press into 'metamorphic', and melt into 'igneous'.

days.title: Energy sources
days.work: Label a rock cycle diagram with energy from the sun (weathering, erosion) and Earth's interior (melting, metamorphism).

days.title: Weathering lab
days.work: Shake sugar cubes in a jar for different times to model mechanical weathering and graph the results.

days.title: California rocks
days.work: Research California's state rock serpentine and granite of the Sierra Nevada and place each in the rock cycle.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Draw and explain a complete rock cycle model with at least 8 processes.

weeks.topic: Weathering, erosion and deposition shape the surface

days.title: Stream table
days.work: Build a stream table in a baking pan with sand and observe erosion and delta formation as water flows.

days.title: Changing slope
days.work: Repeat with steeper slope and record differences in erosion and deposition.

days.title: Glaciers
days.work: Drag an ice cube with embedded sand across clay to model glacial erosion and compare to Yosemite Valley.

days.title: Fast vs. slow
days.work: Compare landslides, floods and canyon formation on a timeline from seconds to millions of years.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a CER on how water shaped a California landform.

objectives: Explain why resources are unevenly distributed

days.title: Gold Rush geology
days.work: Read about how California gold formed in quartz veins and concentrated in streams, then explain the geologic processes.

days.title: Aquifer model
days.work: Build an aquifer in a cup with gravel, sand and clay layers and add colored 'pollution' to see it spread.

days.title: Oil and gas
days.work: Read about how oil formed in California's Central Valley and map where fossil fuels are found.

days.title: Resource map
days.work: Analyze a USGS map of mineral and groundwater resources and explain uneven distribution.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on resource formation and distribution.

objectives: Evaluate how resource extraction affects people and environment

days.title: Cookie mining
days.work: Mine chocolate chips from a cookie with toothpicks, track 'costs' and 'profits', and discuss environmental damage.

days.title: Central Valley groundwater
days.work: Analyze data on Central Valley land subsidence from groundwater pumping and graph the change.

days.title: Resource essay
days.work: Write a short explanation of why one California resource is found where it is.

days.title: Unit review
days.work: Review rocks, minerals, rock cycle and resources with a practice set.

days.title: Unit 5 assessment
days.work: Take the unit 5 test.

days.title: Layers in a jar
days.work: Pour sand, soil and gravel into a jar of water and observe how layers settle.

days.title: Play-dough strata
days.work: Build play-dough layers, add a 'fault' and an 'intrusion', and have a family member sequence the events.

days.title: Grand Canyon
days.work: Analyze a Grand Canyon cross-section and order the layers and events from oldest to youngest.

days.title: Index fossils
days.work: Use index fossils to correlate layers between two cliff diagrams.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on relative dating principles.

objectives: Construct a scaled model of geologic time
Explain how time scale is organized by major events
materials: roll of receipt paper or toilet paper

days.title: Toilet-paper timeline
days.work: Build a 46-meter (or 46-square) timeline of Earth's history and mark major events to scale.

days.title: Reflecting on scale
days.work: Calculate what fraction of the timeline includes humans and write a reflection.

days.title: Absolute dating
days.work: Model radioactive half-life with 100 pennies flipped and removed each round, and graph the decay.

days.title: Eras and extinctions
days.work: Read about the five mass extinctions and label them on the timeline.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write an explanation of how rock strata and fossils were used to build the geologic time scale.

weeks.topic: Fossils and the history of life
objectives: Analyze patterns in the fossil record
materials: plaster of Paris or salt dough

days.title: Making fossils
days.work: Make mold and cast fossils of shells and leaves in salt dough and plaster.

days.title: Fossil types
days.work: Compare body, trace, mold, cast and amber fossils using Smithsonian Learning Lab images.

days.title: La Brea Tar Pits
days.work: Explore the La Brea Tar Pits fossils and explain what they reveal about Ice Age Los Angeles.

days.title: Fossil record data
days.work: Analyze a chart of first and last appearances of life forms and identify patterns of diversification and extinction.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Quiz on fossil formation and the fossil record.

weeks.assessment: Fossil models and data analysis quiz.

objectives: Analyze evidence for past plate motions

days.title: Puzzle continents
days.work: Cut out continents with fossil and rock evidence marked and fit them into Pangaea.

days.title: Wegener's evidence
days.work: Read about Alfred Wegener and list four lines of evidence and why scientists first rejected his idea.

days.title: Seafloor spreading model
days.work: Pull paper strips through a slit in a shoebox to model seafloor spreading and magnetic striping.

days.title: Ocean data
days.work: Analyze maps of seafloor age and ocean depth to identify ridges and trenches.

days.title: Review & check
days.work: Write a CER on whether continents have moved, using three types of evidence.

courses.subject: HSS
courses.title: World History & Geography: Medieval and Early Modern Times
courses.description: A chronological and global study of the years 300–1789: the fall of Rome and the Byzantine Empire, the rise and spread of Islam, Tang–Ming China, the West African empires, feudal Japan, medieval Europe, the Maya, Aztec and Inca, the Renaissance and Reformation, the Scientific Revolution, the Age of Exploration and the Enlightenment. Students read primary sources every week, map trade and cultural diffusion, write document-based essays and connect past ideas about law, faith, knowledge and government to the present.
courses.framework: California History–Social Science Content Standards; 2016 CA History–Social Science Framework (Grade 7)

standards.7.1: Analyze the causes and effects of the vast expansion and ultimate disintegration of the Roman Empire.
standards.7.1.1: Study the early strengths and lasting contributions of Rome (law, citizenship, architecture, engineering) and its ultimate internal weaknesses.
standards.7.1.2: Discuss the geographic borders of the empire at its height and the factors that threatened its territorial cohesion.
standards.7.1.3: Describe the establishment by Constantine of Constantinople and the development of the Byzantine Empire, including the split between the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.
standards.7.2: Analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the civilizations of Islam in the Middle Ages.
standards.7.2.1: Identify the physical features and describe the climate of the Arabian peninsula and its relationship to nomadic and sedentary ways of life.
standards.7.2.2: Trace the origins of Islam and the life and teachings of Muhammad, including Islamic teachings on the connection with Judaism and Christianity.
standards.7.2.3: Explain the significance of the Qur'an and the Sunnah as primary sources of Islamic beliefs, practice and law.
standards.7.2.4: Discuss the expansion of Muslim rule through military conquests and treaties, and the cultural blending within Muslim civilization and spread of Islam and Arabic.
standards.7.2.5: Describe the growth of cities and establishment of trade routes among Asia, Africa and Europe, and the role of merchants in Arab society.
standards.7.2.6: Understand the intellectual exchanges among Muslim scholars of Eurasia and Africa and contributions in science, geography, mathematics, philosophy, medicine, art and literature.
standards.7.3: Analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the civilizations of China in the Middle Ages.
standards.7.3.1: Describe the reunification of China under the Tang Dynasty and reasons for the spread of Buddhism in Tang China, Korea and Japan.
standards.7.3.2: Describe agricultural, technological and commercial developments during the Tang and Sung periods.
standards.7.3.3: Analyze the influences of Confucianism and changes in Confucian thought during the Sung and Mongol periods.
standards.7.3.4: Understand the importance of both overland trade and maritime expeditions between China and other civilizations in the Mongol Ascendancy and Ming Dynasty.
standards.7.3.5: Trace the historic influence of discoveries such as tea, the manufacture of paper, woodblock printing, the compass and gunpowder.
standards.7.3.6: Describe the development of the imperial state and the scholar-official class.
standards.7.4: Analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the sub-Saharan civilizations of Ghana and Mali in Medieval Africa.
standards.7.4.1: Study the Niger River and the relationship of vegetation zones of forest, savannah and desert to trade in gold, salt, food and slaves; and the growth of the Ghana and Mali empires.
standards.7.4.2: Analyze the importance of family, labor specialization and regional commerce in the development of states and cities in West Africa.
standards.7.4.3: Describe the role of the trans-Saharan caravan trade in the changing religious and cultural characteristics of West Africa and the influence of Islamic beliefs, ethics and law.
standards.7.4.4: Trace the growth of the Arabic language in government, trade and Islamic scholarship in West Africa.
standards.7.4.5: Describe the importance of written and oral traditions in the transmission of African history and culture.
standards.7.5: Analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the civilizations of Medieval Japan.
standards.7.5.1: Describe the significance of Japan's proximity to China and Korea and the intellectual, linguistic, religious and philosophical influence of those countries on Japan.
standards.7.5.2: Discuss the reign of Prince Shotoku and the characteristics of Japanese society and family life during his reign.
standards.7.5.3: Describe the values, social customs and traditions prescribed by the lord-vassal system of shogun, daimyo and samurai and the lasting influence of the warrior code.
standards.7.5.4: Trace the development of distinctive forms of Japanese Buddhism.
standards.7.5.5: Study the ninth and tenth centuries' golden age of literature, art and drama and its lasting effects on culture today, including Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji.
standards.7.5.6: Analyze the rise of a military society in the late twelfth century and the role of the samurai in that society.
standards.7.6: Analyze the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the civilizations of Medieval Europe.
standards.7.6.1: Study the geography of Europe and the Eurasian land mass, including their location, topography, waterways, vegetation and climate.
standards.7.6.2: Describe the spread of Christianity north of the Alps and the roles played by the early church and monasteries, including Charlemagne.
standards.7.6.3: Understand the development of feudalism, its role in the medieval European economy, and the way it was influenced by physical geography.
standards.7.6.4: Demonstrate an understanding of the conflict and cooperation between the Papacy and European monarchs.
standards.7.6.5: Know the significance of developments in medieval English legal and constitutional practices, including the Magna Carta, parliament and habeas corpus.
standards.7.6.6: Discuss the causes and course of the religious Crusades and their effects on Christian, Muslim and Jewish populations.
standards.7.6.7: Map the spread of the bubonic plague from Central Asia to China, the Middle East and Europe and describe its impact on global population.
standards.7.6.8: Understand the importance of the Catholic church as a political, intellectual and aesthetic institution, including universities and Thomas Aquinas.
standards.7.6.9: Know the history of the decline of Muslim rule in the Iberian Peninsula that culminated in the Reconquista and the rise of Spanish and Portuguese kingdoms.
standards.7.7: Compare and contrast the geographic, political, economic, religious and social structures of the Meso-American and Andean civilizations.
standards.7.7.1: Study the locations, landforms and climates of Mexico, Central America and South America and their effects on Mayan, Aztec and Incan economies, trade and development of urban societies.
standards.7.7.2: Study the roles of people in each social class, the role of slavery and the causes and consequences of warfare.
standards.7.7.3: Explain how and where each empire arose and how the Aztec and Incan empires were defeated by the Spanish.
standards.7.7.4: Describe the artistic and oral traditions and architecture in the three civilizations.
standards.7.7.5: Describe the Meso-American achievements in astronomy and mathematics, including the calendar.
standards.7.8: Analyze the origins, accomplishments and geographic diffusion of the Renaissance.
standards.7.8.1: Describe the way in which the revival of classical learning and the arts fostered a new interest in humanism.
standards.7.8.2: Explain the importance of Florence in the early stages of the Renaissance and the growth of independent trading cities such as Venice.
standards.7.8.3: Understand the effects of the reopening of the ancient Silk Road between Europe and China, including Marco Polo's travels.
standards.7.8.4: Describe the growth and effects of new ways of disseminating information (Gutenberg's printing press, vernacular texts).
standards.7.8.5: Detail advances made in literature, the arts, science, mathematics, cartography, engineering and understanding of human anatomy and astronomy.
standards.7.9: Analyze the historical developments of the Reformation.
standards.7.9.1: List the causes for the internal turmoil in and weakening of the Catholic church.
standards.7.9.2: Describe the theological, political and economic ideas of the major figures of the Reformation (Erasmus, Luther, Calvin, Tyndale).
standards.7.9.3: Explain Protestants' new practices of church self-government and their influence on the development of democratic practices.
standards.7.9.4: Identify and locate the European regions that remained Catholic and those that became Protestant and explain how division affected the distribution of religions in the New World.
standards.7.9.5: Analyze how the Counter-Reformation revitalized the Catholic church and the forces that fostered the movement (Jesuits, Council of Trent).
standards.7.9.6: Understand the institution and impact of missionaries on Christianity and the diffusion of Christianity from Europe to other parts of the world.
standards.7.9.7: Describe the Golden Age of cooperation between Jews and Muslims in medieval Spain and the expulsion of Jews and Muslims in 1492.
standards.7.10: Analyze the historical developments of the Scientific Revolution and its lasting effect on religious, political and cultural institutions.
standards.7.10.1: Discuss the roots of the Scientific Revolution (Greek rationalism; Jewish, Christian and Muslim science; Renaissance humanism).
standards.7.10.2: Understand the significance of the new scientific theories (Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler, Newton) and the significance of new inventions (telescope, microscope, thermometer, barometer).
standards.7.10.3: Understand the scientific method advanced by Bacon and Descartes, the influence of new scientific rationalism on the growth of democratic ideas, and the coexistence of science with traditional religious beliefs.
standards.7.11: Analyze political and economic change in the sixteenth, seventeenth and eighteenth centuries (the Age of Exploration, the Enlightenment and the Age of Reason).
standards.7.11.1: Know the great voyages of discovery, the locations of the routes and the influence of cartography in the development of a new European worldview.
standards.7.11.2: Discuss the exchanges of plants, animals, technology, culture and ideas among Europe, Africa, Asia and the Americas and the major economic and social effects on each continent.
standards.7.11.3: Examine the origins of modern capitalism; the influence of mercantilism and cottage industry; the elements and importance of a market economy.
standards.7.11.4: Explain how the main ideas of the Enlightenment can be traced back to such movements as the Renaissance, the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution and to the Greeks, Romans and Christianity.
standards.7.11.5: Describe how democratic thought and institutions were influenced by Enlightenment thinkers (e.g., John Locke, Charles-Louis Montesquieu, American founders).
standards.7.11.6: Discuss how the principles in the Magna Carta were embodied in such documents as the English Bill of Rights and the American Declaration of Independence.
standards.CST-1: Chronological and spatial thinking: explain how major events are related to one another in time.
standards.CST-3: Chronological and spatial thinking: use a variety of maps and documents to identify physical and cultural features and explain historical migration and the diffusion of ideas and goods.
standards.REP-2: Research, evidence and point of view: distinguish relevant from irrelevant information, essential from incidental, and verifiable from unverifiable.
standards.REP-4: Research, evidence and point of view: assess the credibility of primary and secondary sources and draw sound conclusions from them.
standards.HI-1: Historical interpretation: explain the central issues and problems from the past, placing people and events in a matrix of time and place.
standards.HI-2: Historical interpretation: understand and distinguish cause, effect, sequence and correlation in historical events, including long- and short-term causal relations.

units.title: The Fall of Rome and the Byzantine Empire
units.big_idea: Internal weaknesses and external pressures split and toppled the Western Roman Empire, while the Byzantine Empire preserved and transformed Roman traditions.

units.title: The Rise and Spread of Islam
units.big_idea: Islam arose in Arabia and spread across three continents, creating trade networks and a golden age of learning.

units.title: Imperial China: Tang to Ming
units.big_idea: Chinese dynasties built a powerful bureaucratic state and inventions that changed the world, alternating between openness and isolation.

units.title: West African Empires: Ghana and Mali
units.big_idea: Trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt built powerful West African empires and spread Islam and Arabic learning.

units.title: Medieval Japan
units.big_idea: Japan adapted Chinese and Korean ideas into a distinctive culture and a military society led by shoguns and samurai.

units.title: Medieval Europe
units.big_idea: Feudalism, the Church, and new legal ideas shaped medieval Europe, while Crusades and plague transformed it.

units.title: Maya, Aztec and Inca Civilizations
units.big_idea: Mesoamerican and Andean civilizations adapted to diverse environments with remarkable achievements before Spanish conquest.

units.title: Renaissance and Reformation
units.big_idea: Renewed classical learning, trade and printing sparked a cultural rebirth and challenges to Church authority that reshaped Europe.

units.title: Scientific Revolution, Exploration and Enlightenment
units.big_idea: New ways of knowing, global voyages and Enlightenment ideas transformed economies and inspired democratic government.

courses.subject: WL
courses.title: Spanish 1A
courses.description: Spanish 1A is the first half of Spanish I, taking students from Novice Low to Novice Mid. Students learn greetings, numbers, dates, time, weather, personal description with ser, likes with gustar, school vocabulary, food, family, places in town, and present-tense regular -ar/-er/-ir verbs plus tener, estar, and ir (with ir a + infinitive). Culture threads include the 21 Spanish-speaking countries, greeting customs, school life, regional foods, family naming customs, and town plazas. Spanish 1B in grade 8 completes Spanish I.
courses.framework: 2019 California World Languages Standards; 2020 CA World Languages Framework (Novice Low to Novice Mid)

standards.WL-COMM1-NL: Interpretive communication (Novice Low): recognize familiar words and memorized phrases in simple spoken and written texts.
standards.WL-COMM2-NL: Interpersonal communication (Novice Low): greet, introduce oneself, and answer simple questions using memorized words and phrases.
standards.WL-COMM3-NL: Presentational communication (Novice Low): present basic information about oneself using memorized words and phrases.
standards.WL-COMM1-NM: Interpretive communication (Novice Mid): understand words, phrases, and some simple sentences in texts on familiar topics.
standards.WL-COMM2-NM: Interpersonal communication (Novice Mid): exchange information on familiar topics using practiced phrases and simple questions.
standards.WL-COMM3-NM: Presentational communication (Novice Mid): present information on familiar topics using practiced phrases and some simple sentences.
standards.WL-CULT1-NM: Cultures (Novice Mid): identify products and practices of Spanish-speaking cultures and compare them with one's own.
standards.WL-CULT2-NM: Intercultural interaction (Novice Mid): use culturally appropriate gestures, greetings, and forms of address in familiar situations.
standards.WL-STRUC1-NL: Structures (Novice Low): use sound-symbol correspondence, numbers, and memorized patterns to communicate.
standards.WL-STRUC1-NM: Structures (Novice Mid): use gender/number agreement, articles, and regular and common irregular present-tense verbs to communicate.
standards.WL-CONN1-NM: Connections (Novice Mid): use Spanish to reinforce knowledge of geography, science, and health.
